en: The Array of the Basket of the Qualities of Avalokiteśvara.
Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels!
To the glorious Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Āryāvalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One.

1. The First Section: A Description of the Jetavana Monastery.

and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Jñānadarśana; and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajrasena;

having issued forth, they came to the Jetavana monastery.
All of them appeared as if adorned by the vihāra;
the pillars, inlaid with divine maṇi-jewels, appeared as if beautifully decorated.
Gabled chambers adorned with gold were visible;
in every cell, doors made of gold and silver were visible;
and in every cell, stairways made of gold and silver were visible.
There were palaces made of gold and silver;
in the silver palace, the pillars were made of gold and adorned with divine jewels,
while in the golden palace, the pillars were made of silver and embellished with divine jewels.
In a palace made of gold, there were pillars made of silver, adorned with divine jewels.
Outside the Jeta Grove, in front of it, various kinds of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) were seen in the garden;
they had golden stems and silver leaves, hung with various kinds of ornaments.
Various robes and garments were suspended;
silken garments were suspended; hundreds of thousands of pearl necklaces were suspended.

Hundreds of thousands of various crowns, earrings, garlands, necklaces, armlets, and anklets were suspended; pillars with earrings, back-ornaments, and upper-garments, as well as jeweled bracelets and armlets, were seen hanging down.
And there, in that place of delightful radiance, hundreds of thousands of such wish-fulfilling trees appeared.
In that very Jetavana monastery, stairways made of diamond were seen,
and in the gate-chambers, clusters of pearl nets were suspended.
Many hundreds of thousands of lotus ponds appeared;
some were filled with water endowed with the eight qualities,
and others were filled with various kinds of flowers.
Namely: they were filled with blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, vaṭa flowers, and udumbara flowers;
furthermore, various other kinds of wooden flowers grew there, such as campaka, aśoka, karavīra, pāṭala, nirmuktaka, sumanā, gandhavārṣika, and others.
These delightful wooden flowers appeared;
thus, they were seen adorning that Jetavana monastery on all sides.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Jetavana Monastery."
START Kvyu 1,2:
The second chapter, titled "The Drying Up of Avīci.
Now, in that very assembly, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and—

Placing his right knee upon the ground and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he bowed and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, I have attained a state of supreme wonder and amazement.
From where did these rays of light come?"
"Whose sphere of power and majesty is this?
The Blessed One said, "This is not the power of a Tathāgata.
A son of good family, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Noble Avalokiteśvara, has entered the great Avīci hell."
And having liberated sentient beings, he enters the city of the hungry ghosts;
it is for this reason that these rays of light were emitted.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what kind of beings are found in the great Avīci hell, where not even an interval (vīci) can be discerned?"
There he teaches him the Dharma: "In that place, the ground, bounded by walls and ramparts, is made of iron and becomes a single mass of flames immediately upon contact;
it appears like a casket of shimmering jewels.
In that very same great hell stands the Kumbhī, where one cries out in agony."
Into that very cauldron were cast many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings;
just as mung beans or black gram in a pot containing much water boil and cook, rising up and sinking down,
so too did those sentient beings.
In the great Avīci hell, they experience physical suffering.
How then, Blessed One, does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara enter the great Avīci hell?
The Blessed One said: "Just as, noble son, a universal monarch enters a garden made of divine jewels with the great prosperity of a universal monarch’s kingdom,"
In the same way, noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara enters that great Avīci hell;
yet his body does not undergo any change.
When he approaches the vicinity of the great Avīci hell, [he remains as he was].
Then the great hell of Avīci becomes cooled.

Then those wardens of Yama, their minds filled with agitation and being extremely distressed, fall into reflection: "What impure omen has appeared in this great hell of Avīci, now that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara enters?"
Then, lotuses the size of cartwheels appeared there,
and that cauldron burst asunder;
in that very fire-pit, a lotus pond of honey appeared.

Then those men who guard the realm of Yama, having taken up swords, clubs, javelins, lances, maces, discuses, tridents, and so forth, and having seized all the equipment of the Avīci hell, approached where Yama, the King of Dharma, was;

having approached, they said this to Yama, the King of Dharma: "Your Majesty, please know this first: our domain of karma has been completely exhausted and has become delightful, endowed with every happiness."
Yama, the King of Dharma, said to them: "For what reason has even your field of karma been exhausted?
The wardens and servants of Yama replied:
"Furthermore, let Your Majesty know this first: an inauspicious sign has appeared in that great hell, Avīci."
Everything was completely stilled and had attained a state of coolness.

Then a man entered there, able to assume any form at will, wearing a crown of matted locks, his body adorned with divine ornaments, his mind possessed of supreme loving-kindness, appearing like a golden image;
such a man entered there.
And as soon as he had entered, lotuses the size of cartwheels appeared;
that cauldron burst open,
and in that very fire-pit, a lotus pond of honey appeared.
Then Yama, the King of Dharma, fell into reflection: "Whose power is this?
Is it that of Maheśvara, who possesses great supernatural might, or perhaps that of Nārāyaṇa, who is venerated by the five great oceans?"
Or has such a distinction of fruit come about through the granting of a boon even by other sons of the gods possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*),
who have arrived here upon this earth?
Or has some *rākṣasa* arisen who is a rival to the great Rāvaṇa?
Thus, remaining there, he reflected;
and having surveyed with his divine eye, he saw that host of gods and wondered, "To whom else could such a boon belong?
Then he looked again toward the great Avīci hell.
Having looked, he saw only the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara right there in that great hell, Avīci.
Then Yama, the King of Dharma, approached the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and began to offer a special hymn of praise:
"Homage be to Avalokiteśvara!"
To Maheśvara, to Padmaśrī,
to Varada.
To the one who brings others under his control, to the one who grants the excellent eye upon the earth,
to the one who provides consolation to the world.
To the one with a hundred thousand arms, to the one with a hundred thousand times ten million eyes,
to the eleven-headed one.
To the one whose domain extends as far as the Mare’s Mouth,
who is fond of the Dharma,
and who effects the liberation of all sentient beings.
To the one who has the hands that reassure the tortoises, crocodiles, fish, and horses;
to the one who possesses the supreme hand that is a mass of wisdom;
to the giver of what is dear.
To Ratnaśrī, to Uttamā,
and to Avīcisaṃśoṣaṇakarā.
To the one adorned with the glory of wisdom,
to the lover of wisdom,
to the one worshipped and saluted by all the gods.
To her who is worthy of veneration,
who grants fearlessness, and who kindles the lamp of the Dharma.
To her who possesses a form at will,
who has the form of a gandharva,
and who is mounted upon a mountain of gold.
To him whose nature is as profound as the belly of the ocean,
who has attained union with the ultimate truth,
and who makes himself manifest before one's eyes.
interspersed with many hundreds of thousands of samādhis,
producing delight,
and with limbs variegated [with marks],
To the one who acts for the benefit of the foremost of sages;
to the one who grants liberation from the fear of imprisonment, shackles, and bonds on the path;
to the one who is endowed with the non-substantiality of all sentient beings.
conducive to a large retinue, productive of accumulation,
and like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
To the one who reveals the path to nirvāṇa,
who causes the city of hungry ghosts to wither away,
and who acts as a parasol for the world;
To the one who brings liberation from disease,
to the one for whom the Naga kings Nanda and Upananda fashioned a sacrificial thread,
and to the one who manifests the Amoghapāśa [sūtra].
To him who is strewn with hundreds of manifold mantras, who causes Vajrapāṇi to flee,
who terrifies the three worlds, and who strikes terror into yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, kūṣmāṇḍas, and apasmāras.
To him with eyes as beautiful as blue lotuses,
to the one of profound and steadfast intellect,
to the Lord of Knowledge.
To the one who brings liberation from all afflictions,
who has accumulated the various paths to enlightenment,
and who has ascended the supreme path to deliverance.
It is accumulated through the basis, the mind, and the path to enlightenment; it effects liberation from the realm of hungry ghosts;
and it is strewn with hundreds of thousands of samādhis as numerous as atoms of dust.
Thus, having applied his attention with even greater particularity, Yama, the King of Dharma, again circumambulated [the Blessed One] three times to the right and departed from that very spot.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Drying Up of Avīci."
START Kvyu 1,3: The third chapter, on the liberation of the realm of sentient beings.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara come?"
The Blessed One said: "O son of good family, this one has emerged from the great Avīci hell and entered the city of the pretas.

There, many hundreds of thousands of pretas were running before him—having the appearance of burnt pillars, with bodies as tall as skeletal frames, resembling the hollows of mountains, and with mouths like the eye of a needle.
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara approached the city of the pretas,"
Then that city of the pretas becomes cooled,
that thunderbolt of diamond is pacified,
and that gatekeeper, his slingshot suspended and his hand clutching deadly *kālakūṭa* poison, has blood-red eyes.
By the power of this [meditation], he constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, thinking: "I have no need for such a field of action."

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Āryāvalokiteśvara, having seen that assembly of beings, gave rise to a mind of great compassion; from his ten fingers he brought forth ten Vaitaraṇī rivers, and from his ten toes he brought forth ten Vaitaraṇī rivers.

With a mind overcome by extreme compassion, from all the pores of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s body there issued great rivers filled with the water of the eightfold virtues for those beings.
They emerge;
and when those preta-beings taste that water, their throats then become wide.
Their limbs become fully developed, and they are thoroughly satisfied by that food which is endowed with the most excellent of divine flavors.
Then, even while maintaining human consciousness, they reflect upon worldly concerns, thinking: "Oh, how happy are those humans of Jambudvīpa!"
Happy are those people of Jambudvīpa who enjoy cool shade—
those who constantly provide for and attend to their mother and father.
Happy are those good persons who constantly and perpetually seek out a spiritual friend and maintain their protection;
those good persons are truly conscious who constantly and perpetually immerse themselves in the Mahāyāna.
Those are true persons who dwell for the sake of the noble path;
those are true persons who strike the drum of the Dharma;
those are true persons who restore monasteries that are broken and dilapidated.
They cause them to be restored. Those are virtuous persons who repair ancient stūpas and images that have become cracked, broken, or fallen into ruin.

Those are virtuous persons who constantly and continuously serve and attend upon the preachers of the Dharma, the scribes, the upholders, and the reciters of this King of Sūtras, as well as the Śrāvakas.

Those are virtuous persons who behold the various miracles of the Tathāgata, the promenades of the Tathāgata, and the lakes of the Dharma; those are virtuous persons who behold the promenades of the Pratyekabuddhas;
those are virtuous persons who behold the promenades of the Arhats.
Those are virtuous persons who behold the promenades that are the miraculous transformations of Bodhisattvas.
Having thus reflected upon the realm of hungry ghosts within their own bodies, they renounce the arising of mental desires.
Then, from him, the sound of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the jewel-king of Mahāyāna sūtras, issues forth.

Then, having shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity—which had risen with its twenty peaks—all of them were reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī; they were reborn as bodhisattvas named Ākāṅkṣitamukha. Then, when those realms of sentient beings had been liberated by Avalokiteśvara and were thoroughly liberated,
When all those sentient beings have been reborn on the stage of a bodhisattva,
he then emerges once again from that city of hungry ghosts.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Realm of Sentient Beings."
START Kvyu 1,4: The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Origin of the Moon and Other [Celestial Bodies].
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One,..."
“Does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara still not come?
The Blessed One said, “Noble son, he brings to maturity many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings;
day after day he comes and brings them to maturity.”
Noble son, even the Tathāgatas do not possess such eloquence as that of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Āryāvalokiteśvara.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said, "In what manner, Blessed One?

The Blessed One replied, "Long ago, noble son, a Tathāgata named Vipaśyin arose in the world— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, is the teacher of both gods and humans.
At that time, at that very moment, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, I was a merchant’s son named Sugandhamukha.
Then, in the presence of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, I heard the proclamation of the virtues of the noble Avalokiteśvara.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, what kind of proclamation of qualities have you heard?
Proclaim all of these!
O King of the Wise, O Blessed One, awaken me!"
O Blessed One, such is the proclamation of the qualities of the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara that you have heard.
The Blessed One said: "From his two eyes, the moon and sun were born; from his forehead, Maheśvara was born."
From his aggregates (skandhas) came Brahmā and the others;
from his heart came Nārāyaṇa; from his two fangs came Sarasvatī.
From his mouth the winds were born;
from his two feet, the earth;
and from his belly, Varuṇa.

When these gods had been born from the body of the noble Avalokiteśvara, then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said this to the divine son Maheśvara: "O Maheśvara, when the Kali age has arrived, you shall become Maheśvara.
Arising within the realm of suffering beings, you shall be designated as the primordial god, the creator and the maker."
All those beings who engage in conversation with such ordinary worldlings will be deprived of the path to enlightenment.
They say that space is the *liṅga* and the earth is its pedestal;
it is called the *liṅga* because it is the abode of all beings by way of its play (*līlayā*).
"O son of good family, it was from the presence of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin that I heard such a description of the qualities of the noble Avalokiteśvara."

Having passed beyond that as well, there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śikhī— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
At that time, at that very moment, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, I was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Dānaśūra.
From that Tathāgata Śikhin, he heard the proclamation of the qualities of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Moon and Others."
START Kvyu 1,5:
The fifth chapter, "The Emanation of Various Rays.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what kind of proclamation of the qualities of Avalokiteśvara have you heard?"
The Blessed One said: When all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, asuras, maruts, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans had assembled and were seated together,
the Blessed One, having seen that great assembly, began to deliver a discourse on the Dharma in the midst of those congregations.
Then, from the Blessed One’s mouth, rays of light of various colors issued forth.
That is to say—blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal, silver, gold, and many kinds of rays issued forth.

Having issued forth, they illuminated all the world-systems in the ten directions and intermediate points; then, returning once more, they circumambulated the Blessed One Śikhin three times to the right and re-entered the Blessed One’s mouth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Emanation of Various Rays.
This concludes the first section, titled "The Dialogue with Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin."
START Kvyu 1,6: The Sixth Chapter, The Dialogue with the Tathāgata.
Now, in that very assembly, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Ratnapāṇi rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and—
Having placed his right knee upon the ground and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he bowed and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"For what reason, Blessed One?"
"Has such a sign appeared and been shown?
The Blessed One said, "Noble son, this is Avalokiteśvara coming from the world-system Sukhāvatī; as he approaches, this sign has appeared and been shown by me."
Then the bodhisattva named Ratnapāṇi said, "What are those signs like?
May the Blessed One show them.
The Blessed One said, "When, noble son, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara approaches,"
Then various wish-fulfilling trees spread forth,
mango trees spread forth,
and kunda flowers were constantly produced.
The campaka trees bow down;
lotus ponds appear, strewn with an abundance of flowers;
and hundreds of jewel-trees are seen there.
Various rains of flowers fall,
and rains of jewels pour down;
and various kinds of gems, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, and copper rain down.
And rains of divine garments fell;
right there, near that monastery, the seven jewels appeared, namely:
the elephant-jewel, the gem-jewel, the horse-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel.
Thus the seven precious jewels appeared;
the earth was seen shining with the luster of gold when the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara emerged from the world-system Sukhāvatī.
Then the entire earth shook in six ways.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, for whom are these omens?
The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Āryāvalokiteśvara is approaching; such auspicious omens as these have appeared for him."
When he moved, a delightful rain of lotuses fell.
Then Avalokiteśvara, taking thousand-petaled lotuses with golden stalks that shone like beryl, approached the Blessed One.

Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and presented those lotuses to him, saying: "These, Blessed One, were sent by the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
They were sent forth.
That Tathāgata inquired after his freedom from illness, his lightness of body, and his dwelling in comfort;
then the Blessed One, having taken the lotuses, placed them on his left side.

Then he proclaimed the virtues of the noble Avalokiteśvara: "O Avalokiteśvara, what kind of field of action have you accomplished among those who are always reborn as hungry ghosts, those born in the Avīci hell, those beings born in the Kālasūtra and Raurava hells,
and in the Mahānaraka hells such as Hāhava, Tapana, and Pretāyana?"
In the great hell Agnighaṭa,
in the great hell Śālmalī,
and in the great hell Andhakāla.

In the great hell Śītodaka—and likewise in other great hells as well—I have seen the field of karma of those beings who have been reborn there; having seen it, I have brought beings to maturity there, and I must continue to do so. Having done so, all of them must be established in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, you should not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until all sentient beings throughout the ten directions who have been born in unfavorable conditions have been established in the realm of nirvana, which is without specific form.
Then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, having delivered this discourse in response to the question, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed to one side;
having departed, he vanished into the sky like a blazing mass of fire.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Discourse of the Tathāgata."
START Kvyu 1,7:
(Vaidya 267) The seventh chapter, the Exposition of the Mass of Merit of Avalokiteśvara.

Then the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I would like to ask a question concerning the explanation of the teaching: what is the nature of the accumulation of merit belonging to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family."
I shall explain the measure of the accumulation of merit from merely grasping the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.

It is as follows, noble son: suppose there were some beings, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, who were Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; and suppose they were honored with divine kalpa-long-lasting flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags of various kinds.
They are attended with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
and whatever mass of merit arises from those Tathāgatas,
that mass of merit is contained within a single hair-tip of Avalokiteśvara.
It is like this, noble son: suppose that for a year consisting of twelve months, rain were to fall day and night without interruption over the four great continents;
it would be possible to count each individual drop.
But, noble son, it is not possible for me to count the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.
For example, noble son, the great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth, immeasurable in its vastness,
and extends as far as the Mare’s Mouth.
Therefore, it is possible for me to count each single drop;
however, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the accumulation of merit of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.

It is just as if, noble son, there were all the four-footed creatures in the four great continents—lions, tigers, bears, hyenas, deer, camels, jackals, and so forth, as well as cattle, donkeys, livestock, elephants, horses, and buffaloes.
Among these four-footed creatures, I am able to count every single hair;
yet, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the accumulation of merit of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.

For example, noble son, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to construct stupas made of divine gold and jewels for Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as atoms of dust.
Having had them made, one should perform the rite of depositing them into meditation on a single day;
O son of good family, it is possible for me to calculate the mass of merit in the making of those Tathāgatas made of gold and silver,
but, O son of good family, it is not possible to calculate the accumulation of merit of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Noble son, it is as if I were able to count every single leaf in a forest of trees,
yet I am not able to count the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.

Noble son, it is as if all the men, women, boys, and girls in the four great continents were to [attain] the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddhahood...
I would employ them;
and whatever mass of merit there is in these,
that mass of merit belongs to Avalokiteśvara, as previously described before the child.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Mass of Merit of Avalokiteśvara."
START Kvyu 1,8:
The Eighth Chapter, the Instruction on the Dharma for Those to be Converted.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, nowhere have I ever seen or heard of such an inconceivable mass of merit belonging to the Tathāgatas."
Or even before he became a bodhisattva, such was the mass of merit belonging to the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, suppose there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā who were like me."
And they should maintain them in one place for their honor, providing divine garments, alms-bowls, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick for a full kalpa;
and those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would all be assembled together in one spot.
No one is able to calculate the mass of merit of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
How much less so, noble son, could I, dwelling alone in this world-system, be able to express his mass of merit in words?
Moreover, noble son, all the Tathāgatas have spoken these words with ten voices: "Those beings in the world who keep in mind the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara become happy;
they are completely liberated from old age, death, sickness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and dejection."
They do not experience the suffering of the final cycle of existence;
like royal swans with white, pale wings, or like those moving by the force of a swift wind, they go to the world-system of Sukhāvatī into the presence of the Tathāgata Amitābha to hear the Dharma.
And having heard the Dharma, the suffering of cyclic existence no longer afflicts their bodies.
They do not experience aging or death through passion, hatred, or delusion; hunger, thirst, and suffering do not afflict their bodies,
nor do they recall the suffering of dwelling in a womb.
They are born within that very lotus;

being filled with the essence of the Dharma and established in constant support, they remain in this world-system as long as the firm vow of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is not fulfilled— that all sentient beings be liberated from all sufferings until [their attainment] of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They do not become established.

Then the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi said this to the Blessed One: "At what time, O Blessed One, will he fulfill this firm vow of yours, so that all sentient beings may be established on the path to liberation?
The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, for many reasons sentient beings wander through saṃsāra because of those very causes."
The deity brings sentient beings to maturity and demonstrates the path to awakening to those beings;
in whatever form the beings to be converted may require, [the deity appears in that form].
He teaches the Dharma in various forms:
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a Tathāgata, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a Tathāgata;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a Pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a Pratyekabuddha.

To those beings who are to be disciplined by the state of an Arhat, he teaches the Dharma in the form of an Arhat; to those beings who are to be disciplined as Bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a Bodhisattva;
and to those beings who are to be disciplined by Maheśvara, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Maheśvara.
To those beings who are to be disciplined by Nārāyaṇa, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Nārāyaṇa; to those beings who are to be disciplined by Brahmā, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Brahmā;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by Indra, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Indra.

To those beings who are to be disciplined by the form of the sun, he teaches the Dharma in the form of the sun; to those beings who are to be disciplined by the form of the moon, he teaches the Dharma in the form of the moon;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by the form of fire, he teaches the Dharma in the form of fire.
To those beings who are to be disciplined by Varuṇa, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Varuṇa; to those beings who are to be disciplined by Vāyu, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Vāyu;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by Nāga, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Nāga.
To those beings who are to be disciplined by the Lord of Obstacles, he teaches the Dharma in the form of the Lord of Obstacles;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a yakṣa, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a yakṣa;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by Vaiśravaṇa, he teaches the Dharma in the form of Vaiśravaṇa.
To those beings who are to be converted by a king, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a king;
to those beings who are to be converted by a royal soldier, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a royal soldier;
to those beings who are to be converted by a mother or father, he teaches the Dharma in the form of a mother or father.
In whatever manner beings who are to be disciplined may require it, in that very manner he teaches the Dharma through his form.
In this way, noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
He brings them to maturity and points out the ground of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Dharma for Those to be Converted."
START Kvyu 1,9:
The ninth chapter, the Consolation of the Asuras.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, I have attained a state of supreme wonder and amazement."
And never before have we seen or heard of such a domain as the domain of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara;
even among the Tathāgatas, nothing of such a kind exists.
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, in this very Jambudvīpa there is a cave named Vajrakukṣi.
Here, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asuras used to dwell.
There, noble son, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, in the form of an asura, teaches the Dharma to the asuras."
And he expounded this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras.
To the asuras who had come to hear the Dharma, he spoke thus: "O asuras, listen to the Dharma!

And you others who are in the assembly of asuras, with minds of loving-kindness, peaceful minds, and compassionate minds, and having directed thoughts toward the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, [listen to] this Dharma discourse, the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*."
It should be heard.
Then those asuras, with palms joined in reverence, listened to this Dharma discourse in the presence of Avalokiteśvara:
"Blessed are those in the world who bring face-to-face and listen to such a Mahāyāna sūtra, the King of Jewels, the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem."
And having heard it, they will have faith in it, accept it, and write it down.
They will cause it to be written, they will uphold it, and they will recite it.
They will worship it,
they will contemplate it,
and they will reveal it in detail to others.
They will cultivate [this practice], and with supreme joy, reverence, and resolute intention, they will pay homage; and for them,
the five deeds of immediate retribution will be exhausted.
Having exhausted [their defilements], they will possess purified bodies and remember their past lives;
at the time of death, twelve Tathāgatas will approach them.
And all those Tathāgatas will comfort you, saying: "Do not fear, noble son!
You have heard the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras.
You have prepared various paths for the sake of going to Sukhāvatī."
In that world-system Sukhāvatī, for your sake, a variegated parasol and a lion-throne have been prepared;
divine crowns, earrings, and garlands are such signs [of your arrival].
At the very moment death occurs, you will indeed follow after Sukhāvatī.
Thus, Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, demonstrating a most distinguished fruit of merit, revealed the stage of nirvāṇa;
he revealed the path to nirvāṇa for the asuras in order to turn them away from all evil thoughts and to establish them on the unsurpassed path to enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from that very place.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Consolation of the Asuras."
START Kvyu 1,10:
The tenth chapter, on the manifestation of the golden ground and so forth.

Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, it is exceedingly rare to hear of these miraculous transformations and the exaltation of the virtues of this Avalokiteśvara."
The Blessed One said: "Moreover, noble son, when he emerged from that Vajra-womb and entered the ground made of gold,"
Now listen to the proclamation of his virtues.
That too was a teaching from even earlier times.
Having transcended that as well, there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Viśvabhū, endowed with knowledge and conduct.
The Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—

during that time and at that moment, I was the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, a seer who preached patience, dwelling in a mountain cave and a remote hamlet, wandering in a region of the earth frequented by human beings.

Then, from time to time, I heard from the presence of that Tathāgata Viśvabhū concerning the manifestation of the qualities of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, who brings all sentient beings to maturity.

Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, there is a ground called Kāñcanamayī; having gone to that northern Kāñcanamayī ground, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara taught the Dharma to sentient beings who were facing downward.
It demonstrates the Noble Eightfold Path leading to Nirvana.
Having emerged from that ground of gold, he enters a ground of silver.
There, he sees beings and persons who possess four legs.
Having seen them, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara teaches the Dharma to all those beings:
"Listen, all you worthy persons, to this Dharma-discourse directly before you; with minds that are unwavering and pure, quickly contemplate that which leads to Nirvāṇa."
Then all those men, standing before Avalokiteśvara, said this: "Console us!
Be a guide on the path for beings who have become blind;
be a protector for beings who are without protection."

Be a refuge and a final resort for beings who are without refuge; be like a mother and father to beings overwhelmed by darkness and lost on the path. O Sacetaka, through great compassion, be a guide to the path of liberation.
Happy are those beings who constantly remember and recite your name and your vow;
they shall never experience this most intense suffering.
For they release such suffering as the kind that we ourselves are experiencing.
Then he caused the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, to issue from the ear-cavities of those beings.
And having heard this Dharma-discourse, those beings emitted it into the ear-cavities of one another.
Having heard that as well, those men were established in the stage of non-retrogression, endowed with the highest bliss, and perfected.

Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having emerged from that golden ground, entered another ground made of iron with a heart oppressed by great compassion for the sake of maturing sentient beings— namely, the iron ground where King Bali, the lord of the asuras, was bound.
He approached the very presence of Bali, the lord of the asuras; having approached, he came into the range of King Bali’s vision from afar, emitting rays of many colors like a golden image.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Presentation of the Golden Ground and Other Features."
START Kvyu 1,11:
The eleventh chapter, "The Consolation of Bali.
Then King Bali, the lord of the asuras, saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara approaching from afar.

Having seen him, she went together with her retinue of the inner apartments and many hundreds of thousands of asuras, including those who were hunchbacked, dwarfish, and so forth, each with a thousand attendants;
having arrived, she fell at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and uttered this exclamation:
(Vaidya 271)
Today my birth has become fruitful, as have my life and my merit;
today indeed such a desire of mine has been completely fulfilled.
Today my intention has been fulfilled and purified of suffering,
since I have rightly beheld the Sole Kinsman of the World in person.
Then all my happiness will once again be established in desire,
and those beings shall become happy, freed from all suffering.
Released from the bonds of saṃsāra, they abide in happiness and joy;
by my very sight, all their fetters have burst asunder,
and they flee further and further away, like serpents before a garuḍa.
Then King Bali, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara, offered him a jeweled seat and, joining his ten fingers in reverent salutation, spoke thus: "Furthermore, Blessed One,
please sit upon this seat."

Grant your grace; be the protector of those devoted to evil, who are like those born blind, who are addicted to adultery, intent on taking life, harmful to the lives of others, terrified by the fear of old age and death, whose minds are agitated, and who are afflicted by the wicked conditions of saṃsāra.
Be a mother and father to the destitute;
O Blessed One, be a protector of those who are wicked, cruel, and fierce;
be the pacifier of the most terrible and evil beings.
For us, who were bound by fetters, all our bonds and the like have been completely released through the sight of you;
they have burst apart and flee further and further away.
Merely by the sight of you, those very auspicious karmic fruits of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and the pleasures of a universal monarch that belong to me have become manifest.
Therefore, O Blessed One, please show us such a path of Dharma by which we may never again experience the suffering of bondage,
nor may these various bonds ever again come into the range of our vision.

Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spoke thus to King Bali, the lord of the asuras: "O Great King, those who generate a mind of non-violence toward sentient beings, who offer alms-food to the teaching of the Tathāgata, and who perform great service and benefit, [attain these fruits]."
And no sentient beings whatsoever shall cause them any affliction even in their dreams;
they shall write out this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, or cause it to be written.
At the very least, they hear even the name of this Dharma discourse,
or they offer even a single alms-bowl to this bodhisattva.
And for those Dharma-preachers who uphold, recite, write down, or listen to this Dharma-discourse,

whoever shall offer even a single day’s meal, even a mere morsel of alms-food, dedicated to this Tathāgata and this Dharma-discourse, they all shall become recipients of the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
And they shall never experience the suffering of hunger and thirst;
nor shall they ever experience the suffering of imprisonment in hell;
nor the suffering of separation from what is dear.
Moreover, they shall be liberated from all sufferings;
they will go to the world-system of Sukhāvatī,
and having heard the Dharma face-to-face in the presence of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha, they will receive their prophecy of enlightenment.
Moreover, Great King, listen to the fruit of giving.
It is as if, noble son, there are those who present alms-food to a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, whether he is still living or has passed into parinirvāṇa.
I shall describe this mass of merit for them.
For example, noble son, suppose there were bodhisattva mahāsattvas equal in number to the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, all of whom were like me.

Even if they were all gathered together in one place for a divine eon, providing him with every kind of comfort and service, they would all be unable to calculate the mass of merit and the accumulation of roots of goodness from the gift of a single bowl of alms;
how much more so then, when I dwell here alone in this abode of the asuras?
For example, noble son, it might be possible for me to grasp the measure of atoms;
but, noble son, it is not possible for me to calculate the mass of merit from this alms-bowl.
For example, noble son, suppose all the men, women, boys, girls, and so forth in the four great continents were engaged in agricultural labor.
In those four great continents, they would not engage in any other form of agriculture;
from time to time, the nāga kings would send down showers of rain,
and by that, mustard seeds would be produced.
And he should turn that into a single threshing floor.
All those men, women, boys, girls, and so forth— having crushed them all with carts, loads, sacks, stools, camels, oxen, and donkeys— he should make a great heap upon that vast threshing floor.
"O son of good family, having crushed [them] with oxen, donkeys, and so forth, and having produced a great heap, it would be possible to count each individual fruit one by one;
but, O son of good family, it is not possible to count the mass of merit from the alms-bowl."
For example, noble son, suppose Sumeru, the king of mountains, were a heap of birch bark eighty-four thousand yojanas deep below and eighty-four thousand yojanas in height above;
and suppose the great ocean were a sphere as round as a melanduka fruit.
If all the men, boys, and girls dwelling in the four continents were to become scribes,
and if they were to write [this] as far as the limit of Sumeru, the king of mountains—
O son of good family, it would be possible for me to count each and every single syllable.
But, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the mass of merit of that alms-bowl.
For example, noble son, suppose all those scribes were bodhisattvas mahāsattvas established in the ten stages;
even the mass of merit of all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas established in the ten stages could not be calculated against the mass of merit of that single alms-bowl.
For example, noble son, it might be possible for me to count every single grain of sand in the river Gaṅgā and in the ocean,
but it is not possible for me, noble son, to calculate the mass of merit from this alms-bowl.
For example, noble son, it might be possible for me to [count] all the tears of all mothers...
"O son of good family, it is impossible for me to grasp the measure of the mass of merit from that alms-food."

Then Balisurendra, having rejoiced in all that was being taught by the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara— who had become a vessel for alms-food and a vessel for sowing seeds in the excellent field— spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with a face clouded by tears, a throat choked with emotion, eyes filled with tears, and gasping for breath:
“Blessed One, what kind of deed did I, though powerful, perform and what gift did I give,
by which I have encountered bondage in this very life, along with my harem and retinue? I gave a gift in an unworthy field.”
I am experiencing the fruit of that very same karma.
Or rather, even a handful of ashes cast into the field of the Omniscient One results in nectar;
yet, out of ignorance, I performed a sacrifice [with such ashes].

Blessed One, when I— having fallen into the views of the non-Buddhists and with a mind seized by pride— began to perform a sacrifice and undertake a great accumulation of gifts, a cruel beggar appeared at that sacrifice in the form of a dwarf.
To him, I gave up my crown, earrings, flower garlands, and jewel ornaments, as well as my horse-drawn chariots and other vehicles, and my jeweled armor adorned with hanging emeralds.

There were chowries hanging down, pearl necklaces suspended from nets of pearls, covered by nets of pearls, with clusters of pearls forming finger-like tassels, and silver bells bound with gold that were tinkling; and there were thousands of other tawny cows with silver hooves and golden horns, draped with nets of pearls, covered by nets of pearls, provided with offering bowls, and equipped with various wonderful bells and jewels.
There were thousands of such tawny cows,

as well as hundreds of thousands of maidens endowed with the most excellent, deep, and abundant voices, adorned with the various and diverse marks of a maiden, possessing supreme beauty that rivaled even the Apsarases, and decorated with divine ornaments.

There were hundreds of thousands of other jeweled thrones, along with numerous heaps of gold, heaps of silver, and heaps of gems, which were adorned with crowns, earrings, and garlands draped about; with armlets, bracelets, anklets, waist-bands, and upper-arm ornaments; with finger-rings; with resonant strings of pearls; and draped in garments dyed in various colors.
And many garments and ornaments were set out;
many hundreds of herds of cattle, together with their cowherds, were made ready;
and many hundreds of varieties of food and drink were prepared.
Foodstuffs endowed with divine flavors and the finest essences were prepared; numerous staffs made of gold and silver, adorned with jewels, were constantly set out;
and many thrones made of gold and silver, likewise adorned with jewels, were arranged.

There were divine fly-whisks with handles, sandals encrusted with jewels, and many thousands of crowns, earrings, and flower-garlands made of gold and silver, studded with gems. At that time, I, as king, gathered together hundreds of thousands [of people], and a hundred thousand brahmins assembled there.
Many hundreds of thousands of kṣatriyas had assembled.
Then, O Blessed One, having seen them standing in that place thus gathered together, I was filled with wonder;
I made the earth have but a single umbrella three times over.
There, I began to give this gift to those who were worthy recipients.
I confess this former evil: that I caused the hearts of pregnant wives of kṣatriyas to burst open and deprived the boys and girls of their lives;
thereafter, I bound all those great kṣatriyas with fetters and shackles.
Having led many hundreds of thousands of kṣatriyas, beginning with the five Pāṇḍavas, and having bound them with the fivefold bonds, they were stationed within a copper cave.
In that very same yakṣa cave, stakes joined with chains were set up, and the hands and feet of those kṣatriyas were bound to them and left there.
At that time, all my doors were made to gape open.
The first gate was made of wood, the second gate was made of khadira wood,
and the third gate was made of iron.
The fourth gate is made of copper,
the fifth gate is made of silver,
and the sixth gate is made of gold.
The seventh gate is made of jewels.
These are the seven gates;
at each individual gate there are five hundred door-panels equipped with mechanical devices.
Upon that golden gate, seven mountains were placed one above the other;
on each individual gate, the mountains were likewise placed one above the other.
Then, I searched for the son of Daśaratha from behind.
On some days in the form of a fly,
on some days in the form of a bee,
and on some days in the form of a boar.
On certain days, having assumed a human form,
and day after day taking the forms of various creatures such as beasts and birds,
I do not see him face-to-face.
Then, having reflected upon this, I commenced the sacrifice.
Then, the son of Daśaratha, seeking an opportunity for descent, went there and uprooted the seven mountains that had been stationed at the gate.

Having uprooted them and cast them aside as if with ease into another region, he proclaimed to those kṣatriyas—Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the Kauravas, and the rest—with a loud voice: (Vaidya 274)
Other kings, having heard the sound they had previously heard, were comforted and remained with their bodies restored to health.
He then said to them: "Are you alive, or are you dead?
They replied: "We are alive, Blessed One."
By that man of great heroism, all those gates were broken down;
then he saw within the copper cave all those kings bound in fetters.
Having seen Nārāyaṇa, they all reflected among themselves: "Has Bali, the lord of the asuras, died and passed away?
Or has the time for our own death arrived once more?
Then they said: "It would be better for us to die on the field of battle than to die while bound in captivity."
If we were to die while bound in fetters,
then our duty as kṣatriyas would perish;
if we were to die on the field of battle, [then it would not].
Then may we go to heaven.
Then all those kings went each to his own home;
at that time, they prepared their respective horses suitable for chariots,
and when they were preparing the chariots, they took up costly weapons.
Then the son of Daśaratha, having manifested the form of a dwarf, covered himself with a deer-skin, took up a bamboo staff and a small stool, and set out toward me. Having reached the gate,
he was stopped by the gatekeepers, who said, "Do not enter, you little dwarf brahmin!"
He replied, "I have come from afar.
Then the gatekeeper said to him, "Brāhmaṇa,
from which land have you come?"
He said to him, "I have come from Candradvīpa, O royal seer.
Then that gatekeeper went and announced to Bali: "Your Majesty, a dwarf Brahmin has arrived at your door."
Then Bali said this to him: "What kind of object does he request?
Then that gatekeeper said this to him: "Your Majesty, I do not permit him to enter.
Then Bali said this to him: "Go, sirs!"
"Let the brahmin be brought.
He was summoned by those gatekeeper men and told, "Enter, great brahmin.
He entered.
A jeweled throne was provided;
Śukra remained right there,
and he was known as his preceptor.
He said this to Bali: "This man of Time has entered within;
you will certainly suffer ruin.
Bali said to him: "How do you know this, Blessed One?"
Śukra said: "I know his motives and signs, having observed them.
Bali asked: "What means should we employ?
Then Nārāyaṇa reflected: "Surely there will be remorse for the gift."
Thereupon Sarasvatī was placed in my mouth;
then he said, "Come, Brahmin!
What is your intention?"
Having entered, he said this: "I beg for two footprints.
Bali said: "If you, O Brahmin, beg for two footprints, three footprints shall be granted to you by me."
Having accepted his gift and pronounced a blessing, he was presented with that which had been offered by him: sesame seeds, water, and gold.
Thereupon, Bāṇa caused his dwarf form to disappear.
Then Śukra said this to Bali: "O King, I told you that this person of Time (Kālapuruṣa) had entered."
And you did not treat your speech with authority;
experience now this fruit of that action,
for by it you have made yourself a great authority.
The moon and the sun were stationed upon his shoulders;
having seized shackles, wheels, bows, lances, and slings, he was fully armed.
Then Bali, the lord of the asuras, fell face downward; having lost his memory, he stood there trembling.
"What have I done? I have consumed poison with my own hand!
I have fulfilled the two-footed [verses]."
A third step does not exist.
Then he said: "A third step does not exist;
that which was requested by me as a gift [is this]."
"What kind of evil am I committing?
Then Nārāyaṇa said this to him: "You must remain wherever I establish you. Then Bali, the lord of the asuras, said this to him: "I shall do exactly as you have commanded."
"Do you tell the truth?
He replied, "I tell the truth, I tell the truth.
Thus he was bound by the snares of truth.
That sacrificial ground was destroyed;
those vessels were defiled with remnants;
and those maidens as well were devastated by the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.

And those golden lion-thrones, divine parasols, sandals, garments and ornaments encrusted with jewels, golden bells, and gold bracelets inlaid with gems— all these, as well as the sacrificial ground itself, were destroyed by the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, who rendered them like tawny [ruins].

Then Bali, the lord of the asuras, having emerged from the sacrificial ground, fell into reflection upon his body: "I, Bali, the donor who has performed a noble sacrifice, have received nothing but bondage for the gift I gave at the proper time. Homage be to the God!"

"Just as that doer and wanderer was led away and cast down into the underworld along with his retinue of harem women, so too have I declared, O Blessed One: 'In the past, at Kurukṣetra, I gave a gift; it is the fruit of that karma that I am now experiencing.
Therefore, O Blessed One, O Protector, be my savior!"
May I no longer experience suffering.

Then Baliṣṭha began to praise the Blessed One, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, with these special hymns: "Be our protection, O you who hold the auspicious lotus in your hand! You whose pure body is adorned with the splendor of the lotus!
O embodiment of Amitābha, I bow my head to you."
To him who wears a crown with a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) in the midst of his matted locks; to him who holds a beautiful lotus in his hand;
to him who is fully adorned by the splendor of the lotus.
To the one who wears a crown of matted hair;
to the one who has brought all-knowing ones under his control;
to the one who provides consolation to many beings.
Out of compassion for the lowly and the destitute;
to the one who causes the excellent light of the sun; to the one who causes the excellent light of the earth.
To the supreme King of Medicine,
to the perfectly pure being,
who has attained the ultimate yoga.
To the one supreme in liberation, to the one who loves liberation,
to the one who resembles a wish-fulfilling gem,
to the one who acts as the guardian of the treasury of Dharma.
To the one who reveals the six perfections,
the one who brings about virtuous intention—
to Avalokiteśvara, this hymn has been composed by me.
Happy are those beings who remember your name.
Those born in the Kālasūtra hell, those born in the Raurava hell, and those born in the city of the pretas—whoever remembers your name—are liberated;
they are freed from much evil suffering.
Those beings who keep your name in mind possess noble intentions;
they go to the world-system of Sukhāvatī,
where they keep in mind and hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata Amitābha.

Then the noble Avalokiteśvara bestowed a prophecy upon Bali, the lord of the asuras: "O lord of asuras, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śrī, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
All those asuras will become those to be converted by you.
In that buddha-field of yours, there will be no word for passion, no word for hatred, and no word for delusion;
the six-syllable great vidyā-mantra will have attained its fruit.
He presented him with a religious gift:
he offered a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and he also offered a crown and earrings set with a collection of various jewels.
Then the noble Avalokiteśvara began to teach the Dharma: "Listen, O Great King!

Those who contemplate the constant possession of human existence—which is eternal, stable, and perpetual—and who constantly think of great wealth, as well as female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, and those costly garments, beds, and seats,"
And as for those vast treasures— stores of wealth, gold, silver, and grain, and treasuries and granaries— those beings who think of sons, wives, daughters, spouses, mothers, and fathers are ignorant;
those who are attached to these things are seen to be merely like a dream.
At the time of death, no one becomes their protector;
when their life-force is being withdrawn, they perceive Jambudvīpa as inverted.
Then they see the great Vaitaraṇī river, filled with pus and blood;
and those magnificent trees, they see them as ablaze, fully ignited, and turned into a single mass of flames.
Having seen them, they fall into [the river].
Then, bound by the nooses of Time by the servants of Yama’s wardens, they are led away;
very swiftly, very swiftly, their feet are shattered upon the great path strewn with razor-sharp edges.
When one foot is lifted, other feet appear in its place.
They are devoured by many crows, vultures, dogs, and other such creatures,
and they experience great hellish torments.
Then, descending from that great path strewn with razor-sharp edges, they are led to where there are thorns sixteen finger-breadths in length.
Then, five hundred thorns enter into each of his feet; he cries out: "This deed was committed by a being who was devoted to the evils of the sensory realms."
Then those wardens of Yama said this: "Sirs,
you did not offer alms-food to the Tathāgata,
nor did you hear the Dharma-gaṇḍī being struck."
You have not taken up the name of the Buddha;
nor have you ever seen gifts being given and rejoiced in them;
nor have you ever circumambulated stupas or images in any place.
He says, "I was faithless, devoted to evil, shunning the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, held fast by evil friends, and deprived of virtuous friends.
They reply, "You are experiencing this fruit of that karma.
Then he is led by those guardians of Yama to show him this place of his own karma.
Then those messengers of Yama, having led him away, cast him into the Great Hell of the Black Cord (Kālasūtra).
They pierce his body with one hundred spears at a time, yet he continues to live;
they pierce his body with a second hundred spears, yet he continues to live.
A third hundred spears pierce his body, yet he still lives;
when they do not cause him to die, they throw him into the midst of a pit of fire,
yet even then he does not die.
Then they are obstructed at the mouth of a heated iron ball and burned;
even their desired teeth shatter,
and their palates burst open.
The throat, the palate, and the heart—like mechanical parts bound by fetters—all these in that body are consumed by fire.
Even so, alas, O King, there will be no savior in the next world.
Therefore, O Great King, you must diligently cultivate merit.
Having thus delivered this conformable teaching of the Dharma, he spoke to King Bali, the lord of the asuras, as follows: "You must remain heedful; you must never again act with negligence.
In this way, this life in a household is corrupted by many faults and causes one to fall into the most dreadful realms of hell."
Therefore, Great King, one who fears evil must be heedful;
thus has the next world been shown.
Moreover, Great King:
As you listen to the teaching of the Dharma from me, your entire mass of evil is completely purified;
you are fully liberated from all the most painful and deep-seated bonds,
and the path for your journey to the world-realm of Sukhāvatī is made perfectly pure.
And there, a lotus throne made of the seven precious gems will appear for you;

sitting upon that jewel-lotus, in the presence of the Blessed One Amitābha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, you shall hear this "Instruction on Infinite Jewels and Great Merit," which pacifies the mass of all suffering and evil, and accomplishes the transcendence of all miserable rebirths.
You shall hear the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras;
and having heard it, you will receive the prophecy regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment right there, and you will obtain a birth as a bodhisattva named *Supariśuddhabodhicittālaṃkāra*.
Until you have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having taught this light of the Dharma called *Sarvadurgatipariśodhana-bodhisattvālaṃkāra-kāraṇḍavyūha* to Bali, the lord of the asuras, [addressed] that king Bali, the lord of the asuras.
Having comforted him, he said this: "I shall go;
today there is a great assembly in this Great Monastery of Jeta’s Grove."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Consolation of Bali."
START Kvyu 1,12:
The twelfth chapter, "The Consolation of the Yakṣas and Others.
Then, Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, emitted rays of light.
There were many [parasols] of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal-colored, and silver-colored.
Having arrived, they stood before the Tathāgata Viśvabhū.
At that time, those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans had assembled.
Many hundreds of bodhisattvas had assembled.

Then, from among those bodhisattvas, a bodhisattva named Gaganagañja rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, from where do these rays of light come?"
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara was dwelling in the abode of Bali, the lord of the asuras; having emerged from there, these rays were emitted.
From that place, these rays come."
They went once again into his presence.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja said this to the Blessed One: "By what means may I behold the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara? The Blessed One replied: "O son of good family, here he comes;
Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, has just now emerged from the palace of Bala, the lord of the asuras."
Then, in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, divine showers of flowers fell;
hundreds of divine *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, most beautiful to behold, appeared,
and hundreds of thousands of jewel ornaments hung down.
Hundreds of thousands of pearl necklaces were suspended;

fine garments from Kāśī and excellent robes were suspended; and many hundreds of flowering trees with red stalks and leaves of gold and silver appeared, along with many hundreds of lotus ponds filled with flowers, most beautiful to behold.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, why does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara not come?

The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, having departed from the palace of Bali, the lord of the asuras, he is going there to a region of the earth called 'The Utterly Terrifying Darkness,' a domain of yakṣas and rākṣasas, a place beyond the reach of humans, a region of the earth that is inaccessible."
O son of good family, in that region of the earth where the moon and the sun are not known, there exists the king of wish-fulfilling jewels named Varada;
and he provides illumination there.
Many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas dwell on that island.
Whenever the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara dwells there, at the mere sight of him, all the yakṣas and rākṣasas become exceedingly joyful, satisfied, and delighted in heart.

Then they ran before Avalokiteśvara, rushed forth, and having run, prostrated at his feet and addressed him: "O Blessed One, may you not be weary or exhausted, you who have been seen after such a long time!"
"You who dwell upon this ground of blinding darkness," he said,
"I have many duties to perform;
I have not cultivated my physical form for the sake of a single sentient being."
Rather, I must generate a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Then all those yakṣas and rākṣasas prepared a lion throne made of divine gold and jewels for the sake of that Avalokiteśvara; it was covered with various flowers, and there the Blessed One sat down to teach the Dharma.
Those yakṣas and rākṣasas led him there and seated him upon that lion throne made of divine gold and jewels.
Then Avalokiteśvara taught the Dharma to those yakṣas and rākṣasas: "Listen, sirs!
Those who shall hear even a single four-line verse of the noble *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of the Mahāyāna sūtras, and having heard it, shall uphold it, master it, and propagate it,"
And those who attend to it with wise reflection—
for them this shall be an incitement toward a mass of merit.
For example, sons of good family, it might be possible for me to grasp the measure of atoms of dust, but [it is not possible to grasp the measure of their merit].
But, noble sons, it is not possible for me to calculate the mass of merit of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Noble sons, it is as if I could count a single drop of water from the great ocean;
yet, noble sons, it is not possible for me to calculate the mass of merit even of a single four-line verse of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of the Mahāyāna sūtras.

Sons of good family, it is as if twelve Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, were to remain in a single place for twelve eons, honoring [this scripture] with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags—
even all those Tathāgatas together would be unable to calculate the mass of merit of even a single four-line verse of this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of Mahāyāna sūtras.
How much more so do I dwell all alone in this land of blinding darkness?
For example, noble sons, suppose one were to build a house or a monastery in each of the four great continents, equal in size to a single continent, made of divine gold and jewels;
and suppose one were to construct a thousand stupas within those houses or monasteries and deposit relics into them all on a single day.
And whatever mass of merit there is from honoring their reliquaries,
a mass of merit far greater than that is derived from even a single four-line verse of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras.
It is just as if, noble sons, five great rivers, accompanied by a thousand tributary streams, were to flow toward the great ocean.
In the same way, noble sons, for those who hear even a single four-line verse of this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the great king of Mahāyāna sūtras, a flood of the mass of merit flows forth.

Then those yakṣas and rākṣasas said this to Avalokiteśvara: "What kind of mass of merit will belong to those beings who cause the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, to be written?
He replied: "O sons of good family, an immeasurable mass of merit arises for them."
Those who cause the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, to be written down,
have caused the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma to be written down.
They become kings.
Universal monarchs become lords of the four continents;
they procreate a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies—
those who constantly maintain the practice of recollecting the name of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of jewels among the Mahāyāna sūtras.
They are liberated from such worldly suffering;
they become fully freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Wherever they are reborn, [they remain so].
In each and every birth, they will remember their past lives;
the fragrance of gośīrṣa sandalwood will waft from their bodies,
and their mouths will have the scent of the blue lotus.
Their limbs will be perfectly formed;
those virtuous persons will be like great athletes, endowed with immeasurable power of merit.
They shall never experience the state of a yakṣa, nor a rākṣasa, nor a preta, nor a piśāca, nor a pūtana, nor a kaṭapūtana, nor the poverty of a human being.
They will be endowed with a mass of merit from serving Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Furthermore,

whatever sons of good family or beings cause even a single syllable, even the name, or even a four-line verse from this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the great vehicle sūtra, the king of jewels, to be written down,
for them the five deeds of immediate retribution will go to complete exhaustion without remainder.
And they will be handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.
And by beholding that which is dear and pleasing to many people,
they shall come to be such that no disease whatsoever shall arise in their bodies;
there shall be no eye disease, no ear disease, no nose disease, no tongue disease, and no body disease.
They will not have missing limbs;
they will not be reborn in border regions, among barbarians, in evil families, as shepherds, as poultry-keepers, or as hunters.
They will be reborn,
and those virtuous persons will possess perfectly pure bodies.
Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara gave a conformable teaching of the Dharma to all those yakṣas and rākṣasas dwelling in that pitch-black darkness.
Having heard that auspicious teaching of the Dharma, some of those yakṣas and rākṣasas were established in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala),
and some in the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala).
Some were established in the fruit of non-returning, some in arhatship, and some in supreme enlightenment.

Therefore, they approached the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, prostrated at his feet, and spoke thus: "O Blessed One, please remain right here; do not go anywhere else. We shall provide you with service and attend to your needs."
And we, right here in this land of blinding darkness, shall create for your sake divine walkways made of gold.
O Blessed One, do not go elsewhere;
how can we remain without seeing you?
Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said this to those yakṣas and rākṣasas: "Noble sons, I must establish many sentient beings upon the path to awakening.
Thereupon, all those yakṣas and rākṣasas rested their cheeks upon their hands and remained lost in thought.
They said to one another: "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara will go from us to some other region of the earth."
Thus we shall become deprived of discourse on the Dharma;
what is to be done by us?
Then the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara set out from that land of blinding darkness.
Then those yakṣas and rākṣasas who dwell in that thick darkness followed closely behind the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, as he went.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said this to them: "Turn back!"
From afar, he spoke thus.
Those yakṣas and rākṣasas, having bowed their heads at his feet and circumambulated him three times, departed from that very spot.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Consolation of Yakṣas and Others."
START Kvyu 1,13:
(Vaidya 280) The Thirteenth Chapter: Wandering through the Abodes of the Gods.
Then the noble Avalokiteśvara, blazing like a mass of fire, vanished into the sky;

having gone from there to the celestial abode, he approached the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm. Having approached them, he manifested himself in the form of a brahmin and arrived.
In that assembly of gods, there was a son of the gods named Sukuṇḍala who was poor and ill-disposed.
Then the noble Avalokiteśvara approached that son of the gods in the form of a brahmin.
Having approached, for the sake of pacifying the suffering of poverty for all the gods, he said this to the son of the gods: "I am hungry and thirsty."
Then that son of a god, weeping, said this to the brahmin: "O brahmin, I do not possess anything at all.
