just as the so-called "cool breeze" son is a source of refreshment.
This speech was related to my parents:
"O Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, such suffering as this was experienced by me when I was the caravan leader Bodhisattva."

Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, it was just as when I was liberated from such fear of death by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, who had become the horse-king Bālāhaka. Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, I am unable to calculate the mass of merit of Avalokiteśvara;
this brief discourse has been made concerning only a single pore of his skin.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Horses."
START Kvyu 2,2:
The second chapter, the description of the pore of the hair.
For example, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, there is a pore of the hair named Suvarṇa.
There, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharvas resided;
they were not afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra,
but were fully satisfied with supreme happiness.
Divine objects appear there,
yet they are not afflicted by passion,
nor are they afflicted by delusion.
They are not oppressed by hatred;
they do not give rise to a mind of malice,
nor does a mind of violence arise within them.
They are constantly and continuously shown the noble eightfold path;
they are at all times seekers of the Dharma.
For example, O Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, it is like the wish-fulfilling jewel named Avabhāsa that exists within the pore of the hair named Suvarṇa.
When those gandharvas contemplate their intention, then that intention of theirs is accomplished.
Then, having passed beyond the pore of golden hair, there is a pore of hair named Black.
There, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ṛṣis dwell;
some possess one supernormal knowledge, and some possess two.
Some possessed three supernormal knowledges, some four, and some five.
Some possess the six supernormal knowledges; and within that hair-pore, there is ground made of silver and mountains made of gold.
The peaks are made of silver, and the mountains are covered with rubies;
such are the seventy-seven mountains.
On each mountain, eighty thousand sages dwell;
and for those sages, leaf-huts resembling kalpa-trees are seen,
with red stalks.
With leaves of gold and silver, they were illuminated by jewels;
on each side of every single pore were four lotus ponds—
some filled with water endowed with the eight qualities, and some filled with flowers.
In the vicinity of that ritual enclosure were divine *aguru* trees,
fragrant sandalwood trees,
and resplendent *kalpa* trees.

They are seen there, adorned with celestial ornaments hanging down—diadems and earrings hanging down, necklaces and half-necklaces hanging down, armlets, anklets, garlands, and wreaths hanging down; they have golden leaves.
Upon each individual kalpa-tree, a hundred gandharvas are resting.

When they utter their cries of withdrawal from worldly objects, the deer, birds, and other creatures are moved to spiritual urgency, thinking: "This is the pleasure and pain of beings in cyclic existence;
how do they experience suffering in Jambudvīpa?"
Do they perceive birth, aging, and death?
Do they perceive separation from the beloved and dear, and association with the unpleasant?
Do they experience many human sufferings?

Thus, when those beasts and birds, having reflected upon their sense of spiritual urgency, call to mind the name of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the great king of jewels among Mahāyāna sūtras, then foods endowed with divine flavors and supreme tastes appear before them,
and divine fragrant objects also appear.
Divine garments appear;
whenever they contemplate their intentions, those intentions are fulfilled.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have attained a state of supreme wonder and amazement.
The Blessed One asked: "For what reason, noble son, have you fallen into such supreme astonishment?
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is when they recollect the name of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras."
The intentions of those for whom such things appear by the mere mention of its name will be fulfilled;
happy are those beings who shall hear, cause to be written, uphold, recite, and master this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras.
And they will attend to it with wise reflection.
Those who cause even a single syllable of this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of Mahāyāna sūtras, to be written down, shall not behold this suffering of saṃsāra.
They are not born into the families of outcasts or dog-keepers;
nor do they possess deficient faculties; nor are they beings who are lame, hunchbacked, with upturned noses, with pendulous cheeks, with hanging lips, or afflicted by leprosy.
Nor did any disease spread to their bodies; they became healthy, strong, and possessed of gladdened faculties. Then the Blessed One gave his approval, saying, "Excellent!"
Excellent, excellent, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, that you exercise such eloquence!

Many thousands of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as laymen and laywomen, have assembled here; by you, such a discourse on the Dharma has been performed.
Since you have displayed such extensive eloquence.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when this question was not yet explained, the sons of the gods conceived an unshakable faith.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval: 'Excellent, excellent, noble son! It is well that you thus entreat the Tathāgata again and again.'"
Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, it is just as follows: having descended from the hair-pore named Kṛṣṇa, there is a hair-pore named Ratnakuṇḍala.
Therein dwell many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharva maidens.
Those gandharva maidens are beautiful, lovely to behold, endowed with the highest excellence of pure complexion, their bodies adorned with divine ornaments, rivalling even the apsarases.
They are supremely beautiful;
they are not afflicted by the suffering of passion,
nor are they afflicted by the suffering of hatred.
They are not afflicted by the suffering of delusion,
nor is any human suffering found in their bodies;
and those Gandharva maidens [offer worship] to Avalokiteśvara three times a day.
They recollect the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
when they recollect it throughout the three times, then all their requisites appear before them.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "I shall go, Blessed One;
I desire to see those pores of the skin.
The Blessed One said: "Those pores of the skin, noble son, are ungraspable and intangible."
Just as the realm of space is ungraspable and intangible,
even so, noble son, these pores of your body are ungraspable and intangible.
Within those pores, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra has wandered for twelve years.
Nor were those pores of the skin seen by him;
even by that one in whose every single pore a hundred Buddhas were stationed, they were not seen.
How much more so others who have already become bodhisattvas.

Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra wandered for twelve years without seeing [the Buddha], and did not see those pores of the skin, nor even saw a hundred Buddhas residing within each single pore; [how much less so could he see the Tathāgata Akṣobhya]?"
"In that case, will I even be able to go as far as the interior of those pores?
He replied, "Noble son,
even by me, while looking and searching for one of his pores, it was not seen."
Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, noble son, this Māyāvī is incurable; he is perceived in such a subtle manner.
He is stainless, yet possesses form, and is great.

He has a hundred thousand arms and a hundred thousand times ten million eyes; he is the one of universal form with eleven heads, a great yogin established on the stage of Nirvana, highly conscious, possessed of great wisdom, the deliverer from existence, noble, beyond perception, wise, and like a reflection in all phenomena.
In this very way, O son of good family, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is neither heard of nor seen by anyone.
Even those who share his own nature do not perceive him when he has gone elsewhere,
let alone others such as Samantabhadra and the other bodhisattvas.
Noble son, this bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara displays inconceivable miraculous manifestations.
He brings to maturity many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas and establishes those beings on the path to awakening;
having established them, he proceeds to the world-realm of Sukhāvatī.
He hears the Dharma in the presence of the Tathāgata Amitābha.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "By what means, Blessed One, may I behold the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara?
The Blessed One replied: "If, noble son, he comes right here to this Sahā world-system for the purpose of seeing me, paying homage to me, and attending upon me.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "I grant permission, Blessed One."
"Is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara coming?
The Blessed One said, "Noble son, whenever there is the ripening of sentient beings, at that time Avalokiteśvara comes first."
Then the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, placing his cheek in his hand, remained lost in thought:
"What is the use of my long life as one devoted to evil, deprived of the sight of Avalokiteśvara, become blind, and set out upon a path fallen into darkness?"
Then the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, at what time does Avalokiteśvara come?
Then the Blessed One, having heard these words, laughed and smiled, saying: "It is not the time for you, noble son; it is not the occasion for Avalokiteśvara’s arrival."
For example, noble son, descending from that pore, there is a pore named Amṛtabindu,
wherein many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods dwell.
Some belong to one stage,
some to two stages, and some to three stages.
Some belong to four stages,
some to five stages, and some to six stages.
Some possess seven stages, some eight stages, and some nine stages.
Some bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling there are established in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
For example, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, within this single pore (*romavivara*) of the Drop of Immortality (*amṛtabindu*), there are sixty mountains made of gold and silver;
each individual mountain is sixty thousand *yojana*s in height.
Now, these mountains have ninety-nine thousand peaks adorned with divine gold and jewels.
On their slopes dwell certain bodhisattvas who have generated the thought of enlightenment for only a single moment.
Upon those mountain ranges dwell many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharvas.
Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, in that pore of the skin where they constantly and continuously maintain the sounding sun, there are many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial palaces,
inlaid with jewels, beautiful, lovely to behold, and variegated, from which hang hundreds of thousands of pearl necklaces.
In those celestial palaces, the bodhisattvas, having rested, engage in discussions on the Dharma. Then, emerging from those palaces, they proceed to their respective walking-paths.
At each walking-path, there are seventy-seven lotus ponds, some filled with water endowed with the eight qualities.

Some were filled with various flowers, being completely covered with blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), night-blooming water lilies (*kumuda*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), fragrant water lilies (*saugandhika*), *māndārava*, and great *māndārava* flowers.

On those walkways stood delightful wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of crimson hue, with leaves of gold and silver, from which hung divine ornaments— diadems, earrings, garlands, strings of pearls, necklaces, and half-necklaces.
Some were adorned with hanging armlets,
while others were adorned with various other hanging ornaments;
and upon those walkways, those bodhisattvas would stroll about at night.
They recollect the various aspects of the Mahāyāna,
contemplate the stage of nirvāṇa,
and reflect upon the suffering of saṃsāra.
They contemplate the essence of hell;
having so contemplated, they cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
In this very way, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, such bodhisattvas dwell within that pore.
Then, descending from the pore named Amṛtavittabindu, there is a hair-pore named Vajramukha;
therein dwell many hundreds of thousands of kinnaras,
appearing most beautiful, adorned with armlets, earrings, and shoulder-ornaments, as well as variegated garlands, jewelry, and unguents.

At all times, these *kinnaras*, noble son, are devoted to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they dwell in one-pointedness of mind, in the Dharma, and in loving-kindness; they are cultivated in patience, contemplate *nirvāṇa*, and feel a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the human condition. Such, noble son, are those *kinnaras* who delight in the Dharma.
Within that very pore, there are many hundreds of thousands of mountain clefts.
Some are made of diamond, some of ruby, some of sapphire, and some of the seven precious gems.
And there, noble son, within that pore of the skin, such signs of the True Dharma are seen.
Within that pore of the skin, there are many wish-fulfilling trees.
There were many coral trees, sandalwood trees, and fragrant trees;
hundreds of thousands of lotus ponds;
and divine celestial mansions.
There are most beautiful and delightful palaces joined with crystal and silver,
wherein such celestial mansions appear;
in those mansions, the kinnaras rest.
Having rested, they engage in discourse on the Dharma; that is to say,
they engage in discourse on the perfection of generosity and they engage in discourse on the perfection of meditative concentration.
They engage in discussion regarding the perfection of wisdom;
having thus engaged in discussion regarding the six perfections, they each walk upon their own respective walking-paths.
Some of these walking-paths are made of gold.

In those walkways and their surrounding areas, there were wish-fulfilling trees with red trunks and leaves of gold and silver, from which hung divine ornaments—pendants of crowns, earrings, and garlands; hanging necklaces, half-necklaces, and strings of jewels.
And those wish-fulfilling trees stood upon that walkway like gabled pavilions.
Upon those walkways, which resembled gabled pavilions, the kinnaras performed their circumambulations;
while walking, they reflected upon the truth of saṃsāra, thinking, "Alas, what suffering!"
Birth is suffering;
alas, what suffering! Aging and death are suffering.
Alas, what suffering!
That too is the suffering of poverty;
it is the suffering of separation from the beloved and desired, and the suffering of not being separated from the unloved.
That too is a more grievous suffering;
and those who have been reborn in Avīci, those reborn in Raurava, and those reborn in Kālasūtra.
They have been reborn in the Mahānaraka hell,
they have been reborn in the Pratāpana hell, and they have been reborn in the Agnighaṭa hells.
Those born among the Vajra-mountains and those born in the cities of the pretas—
of all these sentient beings, this is the most painful state.
And thus those kiṃnaras reflect with their minds;
having reflected, they reflect upon the stage of nirvāṇa.
In this very way, noble son, the kiṃnaras, delighting in the Dharma, constantly recollect the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Whenever they call his name to mind, he becomes present to them with all necessary provisions.
Thus, noble son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is difficult to encounter; he is like a mother and father to all sentient beings, bestowing fearlessness upon all beings.
He is the one who shows the path to all sentient beings;
he is the spiritual friend to all sentient beings.
Thus, noble son, is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Noble son, it is difficult to obtain even the utterance of its name.
And those who recollect the name of that six-syllable great vidyā-mantra,
they are then born within the pores of his skin.
Furthermore, they do not wander again in saṃsāra;
they pass from one pore of the skin to another pore,
remaining in those various pores for as long as they seek the stage of nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Pores of the Body."
START Kvyu 2,3: The Third Chapter, a Description of the Greatness of the Six-Syllable Great Vidyā.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, from where is the six-syllable great vidyā obtained?"
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, that six-syllable great vidyā is difficult to obtain;
even the Tathāgatas do not know it, let alone those who have become Bodhisattvas.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, why is it that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not know it?"
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, that six-syllable great vidyā is the supreme heart-essence (*paramahṛdaya*) of Avalokiteśvara.
Whoever knows the supreme heart-essence knows liberation.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, are there any sentient beings who know the six-syllable great vidyā?"

The Blessed One said: "No one knows it, O son of good family—the six-syllable queen of great vidyās. She is difficult to approach and immeasurable; even the Tathāgatas who are practitioners of yoga know her, let alone those who have become bodhisattvas."

"Noble son, for the sake of this six-syllable great vidyā, all the Tathāgatas have wandered through sixteen incalculable eons, let alone when they were still bodhisattvas; how then could they know it? This is the supreme heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, which wanders throughout the circle of the world."
Someone knows the six-syllable great vidyā.
Fortunate are those beings who are constantly devoted to the recitation and maintenance of the six-syllable great vidyā;
for at the time of its recitation, Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of ninety-nine Ganges rivers assemble.
Bodhisattvas, as numerous as atoms, assemble;
the six perfections stand at the gates.
Furthermore, the sons of the gods from the thirty-two classes of deities have gathered together.
And the four great kings protect the four directions; as do the naga king Sāgara and the naga king Anavatapta.
Takṣaka the Nāga king,
Vāsuki the Nāga king— headed by these, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Nāga kings protect the earth;
as do other terrestrial yakṣas.
And others guard his space;
in each and every pore of that son of good family,
millions of Tathāgatas rest.
Having rested, they offer words of praise: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
You have obtained the attainment of such a wish-fulfilling jewel;
your seven generations of family lineage have been liberated through this succession of births."
And those living beings, noble son, who have entered your womb shall all become irreversible bodhisattvas;
whoever should maintain this six-syllable great vidyā, whether it has entered their body or is on their throat.
Noble son, he should be known as having a body of vajra; he should be known as a stupa of relics; he should be known as the pinnacle of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Whosoever, whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family, recites this six-syllable great vidyā, becomes possessed of inexhaustible eloquence,
becomes purified by a mass of wisdom,
and becomes endowed with great compassion.
Day by day he fulfills the six perfections and attains the consecration of a universal monarch of the vidyādharas;
and to whomever he gives the inhalation and exhalation of breath— whether out of loving-kindness or even out of hatred— [he bestows this].
They all become irreversible bodhisattvas and swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
this applies even to those who touch them merely by the contact of their garments.
May all of them be bodhisattvas in their final existence;
may women, men, girls, wild animals, birds, oxen, buffaloes, donkeys, and so forth— whosoever sees them, even by the mere sight of their eyes—
all of them become bodhisattvas in their final existence.
May they be freed from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and separation from the beloved;
may they become inconceivable yogins.
Such is the exhortation for one who recites this six-syllable great vidyā.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how may I obtain the six-syllable great vidyā?
It is inconceivable to yogins, immeasurable in its meditations, unestablished in anything other than unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and it is the indicator of nirvāṇa."
The entrance into liberation,
the pacification of passion and hatred,
and the fulfillment of the King of Dharma.
It is the uprooting of the fivefold cycle of existence,
the drying up of the afflictions of those in the hells, and the eradication and deliverance of those born in the animal realm.
I wish to hear the inexhaustible exposition of the omniscient wisdom— the tasting of all phenomena and their fulfillment.
Blessed One, whoever bestows upon me the six-syllable great vidyā-mantra, [to them I shall give my own body as a gift].
He would offer him the four continents filled with the seven precious gems; yet, O Blessed One, even if one were to write it down, if neither birch bark nor ink were available, [what could be done]?
And he shall not do so; he shall not make ink with my blood, nor shall he tear off my skin to make birch bark.
Even if one were to break my bones and perform labor [for me], O Blessed One, I would still feel no weariness in my body;
moreover, he would be like a mother and father to me, and even a teacher to my teachers.

Then the Blessed One said this to the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin: "I remember, noble son, that for the sake of this six-syllable great vidyā-mantra, I have wandered through world-systems as numerous as atoms;
I have attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas."
And from those Tathāgatas, not even a single word was heard. At that time,

there was a Tathāgata named Ratnottama— Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.
I shed tears before him, and then that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha said: "Do not, noble son, shed such piteous tears.
Go, noble son, to the world-system named Padmottama."
There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmottama authorized this six-syllable great vidyā-mantra.
Noble son, having departed from the presence of that Tathāgata Ratnottama, I proceeded to the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Padmottama.
Having arrived there, I bowed my head at the feet of the Blessed One and, standing before him with palms joined, said: "May I obtain..."

Blessed One, Padmottama, [teach] the six-syllable great vidyā-queen, by the mere recollection of whose name all sins are destroyed and one attains the difficult-to-obtain awakening— for this purpose I have traveled through many world-systems, afflicted as I am.
"Lest I come here in vain and my efforts be fruitless," [he thought].

Then the Tathāgata Padmottama caused him to recollect the qualities of this six-syllable great vidyā-mantra: "For example, noble son, it may be possible to grasp the measure of atoms of dust, but it is not possible, noble son, to calculate the mass of merit from even a single recitation of the six-syllable great vidyā."
"Noble son, I am able to count every single grain of sand in the four oceans,
but, noble son, I am not able to count the mass of merit from a single recitation of the Six-Syllable Great Vidya.
It is just as if, noble son, there were some man..."
He would make a house one thousand yojanas in extent, twice as much— five hundred yojanas—
and fill it completely with sesame seeds such that not even the space of a needle's eye would remain empty.
There, a man who is neither subject to old age nor death is stationed at the gate.
After a hundred eons have passed, he might cast a single sesame seed outside the gate.
In this manner, it would take a length of time for all the sesame seeds contained within that entire house to be completely exhausted and eliminated.
That can be calculated by me;
however, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the mass of merit from even a single recitation of the Six-Syllable Great Vidyā.

It is just as if, noble son, one were to cause various kinds of crops to be cultivated in the four continents—such as barley, wheat, rice, mung beans, black gram, and so forth, along with sesame, jujube, and horse gram.
There, from time to time, the dragon kings provide showers of rain; those crops are brought to fruition, and when they have ripened, they are harvested.
In this way, he would turn Jambudvīpa into a threshing floor;
then, having transported it by means of carts, loads, baskets, sacks, oxen, donkeys, and so forth, they would cast it into that threshing floor,
and after it had been trampled by oxen and donkeys, it would be formed into a great heap.
"Noble son, I am able to count each of these fruits individually;
however, noble son, I am not able to count the mass of merit from a single recitation of the Six-Syllable Great Vidyā.
It is just as if, noble son, these great rivers were flowing through Jambudvīpa day and night."
They are as follows: the Gaṅgā, Sītā, Yamunā, Sindhu, Śatadru, Candrabhāgā, Erāvatī, Sumāgandhā, Himavatī, and Kalaśodarī.
Each river has five thousand tributaries, and they flow day and night into the great ocean.
In the same way, the mass of merit from a single recitation of the six-syllable great vidyā flows forth.
While it might be possible for me to count every single drop of those great rivers,
noble son, it is not possible for me to count the mass of merit from a single recitation of the six-syllable great vidyā.

It is just as if, noble son, among the four-footed species in the four continents—such as cows, donkeys, buffaloes, horses, and elephants; dogs, jackals, goats, and domestic livestock; as well as lions, tigers, hyenas, deer, monkeys, rabbits, and so forth—
O noble son, it is possible for me to count each and every hair of these [beings], but it is not possible to calculate the mass of merit from even a single recitation of the Six-Syllable Great Vidyā.
O noble son, it is just as if there were a king of mountains named Vajrāṅkuśa, ninety-nine thousand yojanas in height and eighty-four thousand yojanas below the surface.
One side of that king of mountains, Vajrāṅkuśa, measures eighty-four thousand yojanas. On that side of the king of mountains, there would be a man named Jarāmara.
After a kalpa has passed, he would wipe it once with a cloth from Kāśi.
By acting in this way, there would be its complete exhaustion and purification;
for it is possible to determine the measure of these times— down to the years, months, days, muhūrtas, nāḍīs, kalās, and even the breaths.
But it is not possible to calculate the mass of merit from even a single recitation of the Great Six-Syllable Vidyā.

For example, noble son, suppose there were a great ocean eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth and immeasurable in its vastness, extending as far as the Mare’s Mouth; could I count every single drop of water with the tip of a hair split a hundred times?
However, noble son, it is not possible for me to calculate the mass of merit of the six-syllable great vidyā.
Noble son, it is as if I could count every single leaf of a forest of trees,
yet it is not possible to calculate the mass of merit of even a single recitation of the six-syllable great vidyā.
For example, noble son, suppose all the men, women, boys, and girls dwelling in the four continents were each to become bodhisattvas established on the ten stages;
the mass of merit belonging to those bodhisattvas would not equal the mass of merit from a single recitation of the six-syllable great vidyā-mantra.
For example, noble son, suppose that for a full kalpa— calculated by a year of twelve months, or a year of thirteen months including an intercalary month—
a deity were to rain day and night;

In that pore there are ninety-nine thousand celestial palaces made of divine gold, draped with clusters of pearl necklaces and silk streamers, hung with garlands of bells, and illuminated by moonstone jewels;
within those palaces, the forms of Tathāgatas are seated.
They teach the Dharma to the humans of Jambudvīpa;
that is to say, they set forth the exposition of the six perfections,
and they set forth the exposition of the perfection of generosity.
They teach the exposition of the perfection of ethical discipline;
they teach the exposition of the perfection of patience;
they teach the exposition of the perfection of vigor.
They teach the exposition of the perfection of meditative concentration;
they teach the exposition of the perfection of wisdom.
Having thus performed various teachings of the Dharma, they teach the Dharma to the humans of Jambudvīpa from time to time.
In this way, noble son, those beings saw as far as the pores of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
In that very Jetavana monastery,
the sons of the gods— headed by the Mahesvaras, Narayanas, and others, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— had assembled.
Many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas had assembled.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, do those pores of the skin exist?"

The Blessed One said: "Then, noble son, having passed beyond that pore of the skin, [one reaches] Avalokiteśvara’s right big toe, where those four great oceans circulate, yet they neither know nor perceive it.
When water issues forth from the right big toe,"
Then they fall into the Mare’s Mouth;
then they go toward a heap of ashes.
In this very way, noble son, the empowerment of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara exists.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does even that pore exist?
The Blessed One replied: "That too, son of good family, does not exist."
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is Avalokiteśvara not coming?
The Blessed One replied: "He is coming, noble son, Avalokiteśvara, to this very Jetavana Great Monastery, in order to see me, to pay homage to me, and to attend upon me."
The sons of the gods who were companions of Maheśvara [received] a prophecy and an instruction regarding this world-system.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara emitted rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, madder-colored, crystal-colored, and silver-colored. Those rays came to the Jeta Grove;
having arrived, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and then, departing once more from the Jeta Grove monastery, they went to the great Avīci hell.
Having gone there, they bring about a state of coolness in the great Avīci hell.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, from where do these rays come, and where do they go?
The Blessed One replied: "In this way, noble son, various kinds of rays have been emitted by Avalokiteśvara."
They come to this monastery in the Jeta Grove;
having arrived, they circumambulate me three times and go to the great Avīci hell.
Having gone there, they bring coolness to the great Avīci hell.
In that Jeta Grove monastery, auspicious signs appeared:
divine campaka trees appeared,
and divine lotus ponds appeared.
There in the Jeta Grove monastery, divine golden splendors were seen;
such was the Jeta Grove monastery as it appeared.
Then Avalokiteśvara, having departed from the world-system of Sukhāvatī, set out for the Jeta Grove monastery.
In due course, he arrived at the Jeta Grove monastery.
Having entered that Jeta Grove monastery, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Then, with a voice as melodious as the song of the kalaviṅka bird, the Blessed One addressed him: "Have you come, noble son?
Have you brought beings to spiritual maturity?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said this to the Blessed One: "I have done as commanded by the Blessed One."
"In this way, I have brought the field of action to completion.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! It is well that you have brought such a field of action to completion."
Then Avalokiteśvara presented lotuses to the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, these were sent to you by the Tathāgata Amitābha.
He inquires after your freedom from illness, your freedom from affliction, your physical vigor, and your dwelling in comfort.
Thereupon, the Blessed One accepted them and placed them at his left side.
Then the divine son Maheśvara approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and said this to the Blessed One: "May I, O Blessed One, receive an instruction concerning the exposition of the prophecy?
The Blessed One said: (Vaidya 304)
"Go, noble son; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara will grant you a prophecy.
Then the divine son Maheśvara, having prostrated at the feet of Avalokiteśvara, began to offer this special hymn of praise:

"Homage to Avalokiteśvara, the Great Lord, the Holder of the Lotus, who sits upon the lotus, who is dear to the lotus, whose hand holds the pure lotus, the Glory of the Lotus, who is surrounded [by a retinue], who brings delight to the world, and who bestows excellent vision upon the earth."
To the one who causes delight.
Thus the divine son Maheśvara, having gone and performed a special hymn of praise to Avalokiteśvara, remained silent.
Then Avalokiteśvara said this to him: "For what reason, noble son, do you remain silent?
Then the divine son Maheśvara said this to him: "Grant me the prophecy of my attainment of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

Avalokiteśvara said this to him: "Son of good family, in the world-system Vivṛtā, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhasmeśvara— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
Then the goddess Umā approached, bowed her head at the feet of Avalokiteśvara, and began to utter a hymn of praise to him:

"Homage to Avalokiteśvara, the Great Lord, the giver of life, who grants the excellent eye upon the earth, who possesses the splendor of a pure lotus, who is surrounded [by hosts], who has set out for the stage of Nirvāṇa,
the maker of good intentions, the upholder of the Dharma."
Thus, having offered this hymn of praise, the goddess Umā began to address Avalokiteśvara with these words:
"Deliver me from this loathsome female state;
release me from the suffering of dwelling in a womb filled with the impurities of the age, and from being constantly gripped by worldly attachments."

Then Avalokiteśvara said this to her: "Sister, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Umēśvara— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
"Your world-system will be on the southern side of Himavat, the king of mountains.
Then, that goddess Umā received her prophecy.
The Blessed One said: "Behold, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin!
The goddess Umā has been prophesied by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara to attain all of them unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Noble son, this is known as the manifestation named Maheśvara."

The Eighth Chapter.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, Avalokiteśvara has arrived."
Just as one who has become blind regains his sight,
even so, Blessed One, has Avalokiteśvara been attained by me;
today my birth has become fruitful.
Today my hope is fulfilled;
today the path to awakening has been purified by me—
[that path] which demonstrates the nirvana of the Dharma-body endowed with consciousness.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, today please teach us the specific qualities of Avalokiteśvara."
The Blessed One said: "For example, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, there are the two kings of mountains, Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla;
the two kings of mountains, Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda;
and the two kings of mountains, Kāla and Mahākāla."
Saṃsṛṣṭa and Mahāsaṃsṛṣṭa are two kings of mountains;
Pralambodara is a king of mountains;
Anādarśaka is a king of mountains.
The mountain king Kṛtsnāgata;
the mountain king Jālinīmukha;
the mountain king Śataśṛṅga.
And Mount Bhavāna, the king of mountains;
Mount Mahāmaṇiratna, the king of mountains;
and Mount Sudarśana, the king of mountains.
And Akāladarśana is the king of mountains.
Among these kings of mountains, in each of the world-systems, I am able [to calculate] the weight of the kings of mountains— whether it be a *pala*, hundreds of *palas*, thousands of *palas*,
or hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *palas*— even in terms of number, fraction, or calculation.
I am able, noble son, to calculate that;
yet, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.
For example, noble son, it is as if I were able to grasp the measure of atoms of dust.
But, noble son, it is not possible to calculate the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.
For example, noble son, just as I might be able to count every single drop in the great ocean,
so too, noble son, I am not able to calculate the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.
For example, noble son, it might be possible for me to count every single leaf in a forest of trees,
but it is not possible, noble son, to calculate the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.
It is as if, noble son, Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, were a heap of writing materials;
the great ocean were an inkwell;
and all the men, women, boys, girls, and others dwelling in the four continents were scribes.
Even if that Sumeru, king of mountains, were drawn out to infinity,
I might be able to count each and every single syllable; yet it is not possible for me to calculate the accumulation of merit of Avalokiteśvara.

Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, it is just as if twelve Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were being attended by robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all other necessary articles.
And, noble son, the mass of merit from serving those Tathāgatas is [surpassed by] the mass of merit in even a single hair-tip of Avalokiteśvara.
For example, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Avalokiteśvara is endowed with many hundreds of samādhis.
They are as follows: the concentration named "The Shatterer," the concentration named "The Ornamented," and the concentration named "The Dis-ornamented."
The samādhi named Lightning-Eye;
the samādhi named Destroyer;
the samādhi named Great Noble-Mindedness.
The concentration named Ākārakara;
the concentration named Vajramālā;
the concentration named Varada.
The concentration named "Hundredfold Prowess";
the concentration named "Array of the Blind";
the concentration named "Pinnacle of Eloquence."
The samādhi named Rājendra;
the samādhi named Vajraprākāra;
the samādhi named Vajramukha.
The concentration named "Always Bestowing Boons," the concentration named "Liberating the Faculties," and the concentration named "Liberating from Hatred."
The samādhi called Moon-like Excellent Eye; the samādhi called Sun-like Excellent Eye;
the samādhi called Facing the Dharma.
The samādhi named Vajrakukṣi; the samādhi named Sudarśaka; the samādhi named Nirvāṇakara.
The concentration named "the producer of uninterrupted rays," the concentration named "the producer of yoga," and the concentration named "the disperser."
The samādhi called the Excellent Eye of Jambudvīpa;
the samādhi called the Excellent Eye of the Buddha-fields;
the samādhi called Facing toward Loving-kindness.
The concentration named "Illumination of Wisdom," the concentration named "Well-Tamed," and the concentration named "The Letterless Letter."
The concentration named "Drying Up Avīci," the concentration named "Profound as the Ocean," and the concentration named "Hundredfold Retinue."
There is a samādhi called "Revealing the Path.
Noble son, Avalokiteśvara is endowed with these.

(Vaidya 306) "Furthermore, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, in the past, O son of good family, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Krakucchanda, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed."
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
at that time and on that occasion, was I myself, the Bodhisattva named Dānaśūra.
At that time, standing before this Tathāgata, I beheld such a manifestation of the meditative absorption of Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra.
Other great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such as Bhadra and others, beheld the body of Samādhi.
When the bodhisattva Samantabhadra entered the samādhi called Vajrodgata,
then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara entered various kinds of samādhis.
When Samantabhadra entered the samādhi named Moon of Excellent Vision,
then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi named Sun of Excellent Vision. When Samantabhadra entered the samādhi named Radiant Pervasion, [then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi named...]
Then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi called Gaganagañja;
when Samantabhadra entered the samādhi called Ākārakara,
then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi called Indramati.
When Samantabhadra entered the samādhi named Bhadrarāja,
then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi named Sāgaragambhīra. When Samantabhadra entered the samādhi named Siṃhaviṣkambhita, [then Avalokiteśvara entered the samādhi named]...
Then Avalokiteśvara entered the meditative absorption named "Lion’s Play.
When Samantabhadra entered the meditative absorption named "Bestower of Boons," then Avalokiteśvara entered the meditative absorption named "Drying Up of the Avīci Hell."
When Samantabhadra opened all the pores of his body, Avalokiteśvara then uncovered all the pores of his own body.
Then Samantabhadra said this to him: "Excellent, excellent, Avalokiteśvara!"
"You who possess such eloquence!
Then the Tathāgata Krakucchanda said to him: "O son of good family, you have seen but a small portion of Avalokiteśvara’s eloquence.
The kind of eloquence that belongs to Avalokiteśvara does not exist even among the Tathāgatas."
"O son of good family, it was from the presence of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda that I heard such a thing."

Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, by which we, being filled with the essence of the Dharma, may become fully satisfied.
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, those who shall hear the name of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras..."
For them, their previous karmic obstructions no longer exist—

those who were addicted to adultery, those engaged in the occupation of butchers, those who killed their mothers or fathers, those who destroyed the relics or stupas of an Arhat, and those who, with malicious intent, drew blood from a Tathāgata.
Even for such beings devoted to evil, this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of jewels among Mahāyāna sūtras, effects complete liberation from all sins.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said this to the Blessed One: "How may I know, Blessed One, the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, which brings liberation from all sins?
The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, on the southern side of Sumeru, the king of mountains, seven Perfectly Awakened Ones have consecrated two bathing-places called Malanirmala;
these are now consecrated by me."
Just as a white cloth takes on the color blue, so too should that mass of evil be regarded;
in this very way, noble son, this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of jewels among Mahāyāna sūtras, burns away all evils.
It makes them exceedingly white.
For example, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, at the time of the rainy season, all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees become entirely blue in appearance.
Then the nāga king named Śatamukha descends from his abode and burns all those grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees.
In the very same way, noble son, this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, burns away all evils and brings about a state of purity. Those sentient beings shall become happy.
Those who shall hear this *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of jewels among Mahāyāna sūtras—
O son of good family, they are not to be called ordinary worldlings;
they are to be regarded as irreversible Bodhisattvas.
And at the time of their death, twelve Tathāgatas approach and comfort them, saying: "Do not fear, noble son!
You have heard the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras;
you shall no longer wander through saṃsāra."
Furthermore, for them there will be no more birth, aging, or death;
consequently, there will be no separation from the beloved and cherished, nor any union with what is dear.
Noble son, you shall go to the world-system of Sukhāvatī.
"You shall hear the Dharma from the presence of the Tathāgata Amitābha.
In this way, noble son, those beings will experience a peaceful death.
Then Avalokiteśvara bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and withdrew to one side.
Then Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin remained silent,
and those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans departed.
When they had departed, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach me the restraint of training for us.
The Blessed One said: "Those monks who desire ordination should first go and properly inspect the residence."

Having observed [the situation], the monk should announce: "It is pure, Venerable Sir, because it is a separate residence (*nānāvāsa*), and the bones are not present where there is a separate residence;
they are not present in the context of excrement."
It becomes purified.
"In this way, Venerable Sir, it is not fitting for monks to have ordination while residing in various places."
The Blessed One said: "A monk who is of immoral conduct must not grant full ordination, nor should he give the formal motion (*jñapti*).
What need is there to say more? Monks, a monk who is of immoral conduct must not establish a separate residence."
How much more so in the case of a formal motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapticaturtha*).
For these are indeed defilers of the Teaching;
they must not be granted residence among virtuous monks who are worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*).
They should be given lodging in a separate dwelling outside;
likewise, they should not be granted participation in the communal discourse of the Saṅgha,
nor do they deserve the property belonging to the Saṅgha.
And yet, not even the slightest state of being a monk exists in them.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "At what time, Blessed One, will there be such unworthy recipients of offerings?

The Blessed One replied: "When three hundred years have passed after my parinirvāṇa, O Tathāgata, there will be such unworthy recipients of offerings—those who maintain the notion of 'householder' while residing in a monastery."
They will be surrounded by boys and girls;
they will improperly use the beds, stools, bamboo frames, pillows, and bedding belonging to the Saṅgha;
and they will void excrement and urine in the precincts of the Saṅgha.
In the great city of Vārāṇasī, those who use a tooth-stick belonging to the Saṅgha through improper use are born as living beings within the moist earth inside excrement and urine;
those who use a tooth-stick belonging to the Saṅgha with improper use are born among tortoises, crocodiles, and fish.

Those who consume the property of the Saṅgha—such as sesame, rice, kodrava, kulattha, and other grains—by means of improper enjoyment, are reborn in the cities of the pretas. There they possess inferior faculties; their bodies resemble charred pillars, with bones protruding like leaves, covered by their own hair and body hair, resembling mountain bellies, and having mouths like the eye of a needle. Such is their form.
They experience suffering;
those who improperly consume the food, drink, and other requisites belonging to the Saṅgha are born into families of little learning.
They are born with impaired faculties; they are born as those who are lame, humpbacked, one-eyed, or dwarfish;
and they are born as beggars dependent on the faces of others.
Thereafter, they become even more afflicted by disease;
pus and blood flow through their bodies,
and they rise up with their own hair bristling upon their shriveled frames.
Then, masses of flesh fall to the ground and bones are seen;
in this way, they experience physical suffering for many hundreds of years.
Those who make improper use of land belonging to the Saṅgha are reborn in the Raurava great hell for twelve kalpas;
molten iron balls are placed in their mouths.
At the end of the Viṣkambha hell, they are burned;
even their lips and teeth crumble away,
and their palates burst and burn.
The throat, the palate, and the heart—
all these and all other parts are burned entirely and completely, leaving nothing remaining.
Then, monks, the winds of karma blow by which those dead men come back to life once more;
thereafter they are again seized by the men who guard Yama's realm.
Then, for those who have approached their karma and are under the power of karma, a massive tongue appears.
There, a hundred thousand plows are drawn across their tongues.
In this way, for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years, they experience the suffering of hell.
Having passed away from there, they will be reborn in the Agnighaṭa great hell.
Then those men who guard Yama seize them and pierce their tongues with hundreds of thousands of needles;
yet, by the power of karma, they continue to live.
Then, having lifted them up, they cast them into the midst of pits of fire.
Having lifted them up, they throw them into that pit of fire, the great Vaitaraṇī;
yet even there they do not die, and they are reborn in other hells.
As they wander in this manner, three eons pass away. Having died there, they are born in Jambudvīpa as poor people blind from birth.
Therefore, those blameless communal properties belonging to the Saṅgha must be protected.
Those monks who are restrained by the vow of training should wear these three robes:
one robe for the use of the Saṅgha, held in trust for the community.
Likewise, a second robe is for going to the gates of royal palaces,
and a third robe is for villages, towns, cities, hamlets, and market towns;
these three robes, monks, should be maintained.
O monks, those who possess virtue, qualities, and wisdom must uphold these training rules prescribed by me.
Monks, one must not consume that which is not to be consumed; the property belonging to the Saṅgha is like a vessel of fire, and the property belonging to the Saṅgha is like poison.

The property belonging to the Saṅgha is like a diamond; the property belonging to the Saṅgha is like a mountain. It is possible to provide an antidote for poison, but [it is not possible to provide an antidote for] the property belonging to the Saṅgha.
But it is not possible to provide recompense for property belonging to the Saṅgha.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "The training rules have been prescribed by the Blessed One;
those monks who uphold them become restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa."
They become intent upon liberation;
they become intent upon the treasury;
they become skilled in the trainings.
And these are the training rules of the Blessed One.
The venerable Ānanda, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed.
Then those great śrāvakas departed each for their own buddha-field.
And those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans [also departed].
They all departed.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Restraint of Training."
The Blessed One spoke thus,
and those bodhisattvas, that entire assembly, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
This *dhāraṇī-vyūha* of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the king of the jewels of Mahāyāna sūtras, [dedicated to] Maheśvara, is completed.
The Noble *Kāraṇḍavyūha*, the King of Jewels among Mahāyāna Sūtras, is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause;
and also their cessation—thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.
